summary: Mobile IP tunnelling does not work through Network Address Translation devices. This memo adds extensions to Mobile IP and a tunnelling method that let mobile nodes operate in private address networks behind NATs. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: If your phone moves between networks, the internet still has to find it. Special address-swapping boxes break that trick. This memo changes the trick so it works even when you are behind one of those boxes.

questions: how does mobile ip work through nat

subtitle: A UDP-based tunnel that lets Mobile IP traffic pass through NAT devices that break ordinary IP-in-IP tunnels.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP delivers traffic to a mobile node with IP-in-IP tunnels, but those tunnels carry no port numbers, so a NAT cannot map them to the right host behind it and Mobile IP fails across a NAT.
tldr.mechanism: The mobile node or foreign agent asks in its registration for UDP tunnelling, the home agent spots the NAT by an address mismatch and agrees, and data is then tunnelled in UDP using home agent port 434, with keepalives to hold the NAT mapping open.
tldr.outcome: Mobile IPv4 nodes can work in private address networks behind NATs, at the price of relying on unauthenticated address and port fields that open redirection attacks, so short binding lifetimes are recommended.

today: RFC 3519 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says the mechanism will go out of use as IPv6 and Mobile IPv6 are deployed, since they remove the need for Mobile IPv4 NAT traversal.

sections.title: The Problem: Mobile IP Behind a NAT
sections.content:
Mobile IP assumes that mobile nodes and foreign agents are uniquely identified by a globally routable IP address. That assumption fails behind a NAT (Network Address Translation). Mobile IP sends traffic from the home network to the mobile node or foreign agent through IP-in-IP tunnelling, and such a tunnel has no TCP or UDP port numbers for a NAT to use. The RFC concludes that IP-in-IP tunnels cannot in general pass through a NAT.

Registration Requests and Replies are different. They are UDP datagrams sent from inside the NAT, so they can pass and make the NAT create a mapping for the reply. The base protocol, however, does not allow a registration whose source address is not the care-of address, the home address or 0.0.0.0.

The mechanism covers three cases: a mobile node with a co-located address behind a NAT and no foreign agent (FA); a mobile node and FA behind the same NAT; and a mobile node with a co-located address using an FA that sets the 'R' bit, again with both behind the same NAT. It assumes UDP traffic can flow between a port chosen by the mobile node and home agent UDP port 434.
sections.eli5: Mobile IP delivers mail to you in a special envelope with no room number on it. The address-swapping box at the door cannot tell which room it is for, so the envelope gets stuck.

sections.title: How UDP Tunnelling Works
sections.content:
The mobile node adds an extension to its Registration Request to say it can use Mobile IP UDP tunnelling instead of standard tunnelling if the home agent sees that the request seems to have passed through a NAT. The home agent may answer with a reply extension that accepts or declines. After it accepts, UDP tunnelling is available for both forward and reverse tunnelling.

Tunnelled packets from the mobile node use the same ports as the registration request. The source port may change between new registrations, but stays the same for all tunnelled data and re-registrations. The destination port is always 434, and the home agent uses the same ports in reverse.
sections.eli5: Instead of a bare envelope, the data is put in a UDP package with a port number on it. The address-swapping box knows how to handle those, so the package reaches the right room.

sections.title: New Extensions and Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines several new items. The UDP Tunnel Request Extension (type 144, length 6, sub-type 0) is a skippable extension carrying an F (Force) flag, an R (Registration through FA Required) flag, and an Encapsulation field. The F flag asks for tunnelling regardless of the home agent's NAT detection, useful when signalling works but data is filtered. If the home agent does not understand the extension, it silently discards it, and the mobile node MUST NOT use UDP tunnelling.

The UDP Tunnel Reply Extension (type 44, length 6, sub-type 0) is non-skippable. It has a Reply Code, an F flag and a Keepalive Interval. Reply codes 0 to 63 mean assent and 64 to 255 mean tunnelling will not be done. Defined codes are 0 (will do tunnelling) and 64 (tunnelling declined, reason unspecified).

The MIP Tunnel Data Message (type 4) is a small header with a Next Header field. It distinguishes tunnelled data on port 434 from Registration Requests and Replies. The receiver MUST drop a packet whose Next Header does not match the tunnelling mode set for the binding.

A new U flag in the Agent Advertisement shows that a foreign agent supports UDP tunnelling. It SHOULD be set by an FA that supports it and sits behind a NAT, and MUST NOT be set by an FA that is not behind a NAT. A new registration reply code, ERROR_HA_UDP_ENCAP_UNAVAIL, tells the mobile node the requested UDP encapsulation is unavailable.
sections.eli5: The memo adds a few new forms: one to ask for the UDP package service, one for the home agent to say yes or no, and a tiny label that goes on every package.

sections.title: Encapsulation Choices
sections.content:
The default encapsulation is IP-in-UDP, and every home agent and mobile node that implements UDP tunnelling MUST implement it. The tunnel adds an outer IP header, a UDP header and the MIP Tunnel Data header in front of the original IP header. The outer addresses and ports identify the tunnel endpoints. The inner header is left unchanged, apart from decrementing the TTL when the tunnelling is part of forwarding.

Two other forms are supported: GRE in UDP and minimal encapsulation in UDP. They are chosen by the G and M bits, or by a non-zero Encapsulation field using IP protocol values 4 (IP), 47 (GRE) and 55 (minimal encapsulation). A non-zero request must be accepted as asked or rejected with ERROR_HA_UDP_ENCAP_UNAVAIL. Before decapsulating, a node MUST check that the outer addresses and UDP ports match those of the tunnel.
sections.eli5: You can pack the data in one of three kinds of wrapping. The plain wrapping is the one everybody must know how to open.

sections.title: Roles of the Mobile Node, Foreign Agent and Home Agent
sections.content:
The mobile node MAY use the request extension when it has a co-located care-of address, and SHALL NOT use it when registering with a foreign agent care-of address. It must place the extension before the Mobile-Home Authentication Extension so that it is authenticated. If no reply extension comes back, it MUST NOT use UDP tunnelling. When sending tunnelled data it MUST use the same UDP source port as the latest registration request.

The home agent MUST treat a mismatch between the request's IP source address and its care-of address as the sign of a NAT. If the request carries the extension without the R flag and the home agent can and will tunnel, it SHALL send an assenting reply, and it then uses the request's source address as the effective care-of address. If the addresses match, it SHOULD decline unless the F flag forces tunnelling.

A foreign agent behind a NAT MAY add the extension when forwarding a request, MUST place it after the Mobile-Home Authentication Extension, and MUST send the request with an IP source address matching its care-of address. If the mobile node registers a co-located address through an FA that sets the R bit, the R flag is used, and the home agent MUST wait for the first keepalive to learn the correct NAT port. UDP tunnelling is used only for data. Mobile IP signalling is never tunnelled.
sections.eli5: The home agent notices that the return address on your request does not match what you wrote inside. That tells it a box in the middle changed things, so it agrees to use the UDP package method.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
If the home agent does not support the extension, it ignores it and proceeds normally, usually refusing a registration whose source address does not match. When it does support the extension, it uses specific reply codes: 129 (administratively prohibited) when a NAT is detected but traversal is not allowed, or when F is set but forced use is not allowed.

Code 134 (poorly formed Request) is used when the request extension is placed before the MN-HA authentication extension but the D bit is not set, when it comes from a foreign agent after that extension but the D bit is set, or when the Reserved 3 field is non-zero. An unsupported encapsulation draws ERROR_HA_UDP_ENCAP_UNAVAIL, assigned code 142 in the IANA section.
sections.eli5: If something is wrong with the request, the home agent sends back a numbered 'no' that says what was wrong, such as 'badly filled in form'.

sections.title: Keepalives and Lost NAT Mappings
sections.content:
A NAT only keeps a mapping for a limited time, so the tunnel needs keepalives. A keepalive is a UDP-encapsulated ICMP echo request sent to the home agent, and the remote endpoint MUST use two-way keepalives (echo request and reply). The non-HA endpoint MUST send one if no other packet to the home agent has gone out in K seconds, where K defaults to 110 seconds and the home agent can change it with the Keepalive Interval field.

If a mobile node gets no reply even after retransmissions and is still on the same router, it SHOULD re-register so the home agent learns about the new NAT mapping. It MAY then shorten its keepalive interval, but MUST NOT use less than 10 seconds. The home agent MUST NOT try to adapt the keepalive interval itself.

Fragmentation matters too. Because a NAT cannot associate later fragments with a session, fragmentation MUST be done before encapsulation by a mobile node or foreign agent. The home agent SHOULD also fragment before encapsulation.
sections.eli5: The address-swapping box forgets about quiet conversations. So every so often the phone sends a tiny 'still here' ping, and the home agent answers, to keep the line open.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Ordinary Mobile IP security still applies, with one notable change: the home agent must now trust address and port fields that a NAT may have modified and that no authentication extension covers. An attacker can do what a NAT does, so traffic can be redirected to a chosen address. A simple routability check could help against some attacks, but the RFC does not specify one. It RECOMMENDS a short mobility binding lifetime, and its implementation section suggests a maximum of 60 seconds returned by the home agent.

Two attacks are described. An attacker on the path can rewrite the IP and UDP headers of a Registration Request. Or, when registering through an FA with a co-located address, an attacker who merely observes the exchange can send a bogus keepalive while the binding is half bound. The home agent MUST NOT accept a keepalive from a different source IP address than the request, which limits that attack to a bogus UDP port. IPsec can protect confidentiality of hijacked data but does not stop the redirection attacks.
sections.eli5: Because the home agent has to believe the return address on the envelope, a sneaky person could change it and get your mail sent elsewhere. Asking you to check in often limits how long that can last.

fields.desc: MUST be 0 on sending, ignored on reception.

fields.desc: Force: wants tunnelling established regardless of NAT detection.

fields.name: Reserved 2
fields.desc: MUST be 0 on sending, ignored on reception.

fields.desc: Tunnelled data type, using IP Protocol field numbers.

fields.desc: MUST be 0 on sending and verified as 0 on receipt.
